title: How to Handle a Breakup
excerpt: A breakup is a small death, and we keep telling people to get over it like it was a head cold. Grief that is rushed does not heal. It hides.
body:
We do not have good language for the end of a relationship that was not a marriage. There was no funeral, no casserole brigade, no time off work. People expect you to be fine in a week because, technically, nothing legal happened. But something did happen. A future you had started to imagine is gone, and futures, even imagined ones, take real grief to bury. I have sat with people leveled by a breakup who were embarrassed to be leveled, because the culture told them it was minor. It was not minor. Let me say that plainly first.

## Grieve it like the loss it is

The worst thing you can do is rush. We are uncomfortable with grief, so we cover it, with a new relationship, with frantic activity, with the performance of being totally fine. But grief you bury alive does not die. It waits, and it comes out sideways months later in a way you do not connect to its source.

So let yourself mourn. Tell God the truth about it. The Psalms are full of people saying out loud how much they hurt, and God did not edit those prayers out of the Bible (Psalm 34:18). You are allowed to be sad about a real loss. The sadness is not weakness or lack of faith. It is the cost of having loved someone, and that cost is honorable.

## Go quiet before you go searching

The instinct after a breakup is to fill the hole immediately. A rebound, a dating app downloaded the same night, a new person to make the old one jealous. Resist it. A wound you build a new relationship on top of does not heal. It just becomes the foundation of something built crooked.

Give yourself a real stretch of being alone with God and a few good friends before you start looking again. Not as punishment, but because you cannot choose well from a place of panic, and grief is a kind of panic. The person you would pick to stop the pain is rarely the person you would pick clear-eyed. Wait until you are choosing from fullness, not from a hole.

## Resist the urge to rewrite the story

When a relationship ends, the mind does one of two cruel things. It either makes the other person a villain, so you can be angry instead of sad, or it makes them perfect, so you can ache over the one who got away. Both are lies that make grief easier in the short run and slower in the long run.

Tell the truth instead. They were a real person, with real good and real failures, and so were you. You contributed to how it ended; almost everyone does. Owning your part is not self-punishment. It is how you learn something instead of repeating it. The person who refuses to see their own hand in every ending will keep finding the same ending in every relationship.

## Let it form you

There is a kind of person who comes out of a breakup more bitter, more guarded, more convinced that love is a con. And there is a kind who comes out softer, wiser, more able to love well. The difference is not how badly they were hurt. It is what they did with the hurt, whether they let it close them or let it teach them.

God does not waste pain. Romans says he works even this toward good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and that is not a slogan to skip past the hurt. It is a promise to be tested on the far side of it. Ask him what this is meant to form in you. Sometimes the answer is patience. Sometimes it is the slow death of an idol you had made out of being chosen. Let the loss do its work.

## This week

Stop performing fine. Tell one trusted person the actual truth of how you are doing, and then tell God the same, out loud, without cleaning it up. Delete the dating app for two weeks, not forever, just long enough to grieve before you search.

A breakup is a small death. Buried honestly, it heals. Rushed or denied, it festers. Give it the grief it asks for, and it will give you back to yourself, more whole than before.
